headline: August 8, and Washington Is Still Running Its Own Clock
subhead: The canyon that fires early hasn't cooled off yet — yellowfin, mahi, and a scattering of white marlin are keeping the troll and chunk boats busy while everyone waits on the new moon push.
body_markdown:
Here's the thing about Washington that guys from the other canyons never quite get: by the time August rolls around, we're not starting a season, we're managing one. This canyon back in June when Wilmington and Baltimore were still waiting on their water to turn, and now that everybody else is finally catching up, we're just cruising through the meat of it. That's not luck. That's position. We sit closer to the Stream's northern lean than most people give us credit for, and every year it plays out the same way — early June push, strong July, and an August that either holds the pattern or slides sideways depending on what the water to our south decides to do.

Right now it's holding. Boats working the edge and the wall have been finding yellowfin on the troll during the day — small ballyhoo behind Green Machines and cedar plugs, the usual 100-fathom-plus water where the color goes that deep cobalt blue and you can see the temp break if the light's right. Chunking bunker after dark off the drop-off has been the more consistent play this week, though I want to be straight with you — it's not a wire-to-wire bite. Some nights the chunk slick draws fish up fast and you're doubled up inside twenty minutes; other nights you're sitting on a dead slick for two hours before anything shows. That's the nature of August on a canyon edge that isn't getting a hard, reliable current push yet. The tide's building toward the new moon on the 12th, and once that tidal range really kicks in, the current lines along the wall are going to sharpen up, and so will the bite. I'd rather fish the two days before and after that new moon than a random Tuesday in the current lull we're in now.

Mahi have been scattered but there when you find the right piece of structure — any weed line or floating junk outside the edge is worth a stop, even a five-minute stop, because a school of gaffers under a mat of sargassum will make your whole day. Small stuff too, schoolies in the 2-3 pound range mixed in, so bring light spinning gear rigged with a bare hook and a chunk of butterfish alongside your trolling spread. It costs you nothing to slow down and look.

White marlin have shown, not in numbers that make headlines, but enough that if you're pulling naked ballyhoo or small skirted baits on the troll along the temperature breaks, you've got a real shot. These fish are still moving through on their own schedule and Washington tends to get a piece of that traffic earlier than the canyons south of us, which tracks with everything else about how this place runs. Wahoo have been mixed into the yellowfin bite on the high-speed spread — if you're not running at least one bait at 12-14 knots with wire, you're leaving that fish on the table.

Bigeye are the wildcard right now. We're not into the heart of that pattern yet — that usually doesn't build here until deeper into August — but the deep-drop squid chunk crowd fishing at night has started picking off a few, which tells me the door's cracking open earlier than usual again. I wouldn't build a whole trip around bigeye yet, but if you're out there overnight anyway for yellowfin, it costs nothing to drop a bait deep once the sun's down.

Now, the thing worth watching. There's a mild cooling nudge working its way up from the canyons south of us, and if that strengthens and pushes north, it could reshuffle where the bait and the tuna are holding along our edge — potentially compressing fish tighter to the wall, or in a worse case, pulling some of that biomass south with it. We flagged this exact setup last week and said conditions should hold steady unless a shift came up from the south — and that's exactly what's happened. Nothing's moved yet. The water out here has stayed steady, the pattern's intact, and the fish are still where they've been. But I'm not going to pretend that signal isn't on my radar, because if it firms up, it changes where I send people next week.

For the next few days, my money's on the edge holding its current character — daytime troll for yellowfin and the occasional white marlin, mahi under any debris you cross, wahoo mixed in on the high-speed lines, and a chunk bite after dark that rewards patience more than it rewards showing up late. Once we get inside that 48-hour window around the new moon, I expect the current to sharpen and the bite to tighten up with it — that's when I'd want to be out there, not during the slack stretch we're in right now. If the southern cooling signal holds off, Washington keeps doing what Washington does in August: producing quietly while everybody else is just getting started.
